posts.title: If you pitch token launches for a living, watch Friday.
posts.author: James Williams
posts.snippet:
If you pitch token launches for a living, watch Friday.

The SEC votes on "Regulation Crypto," a tailored framework meant to give qualifying digital asset offerings a defined path to raise capital without triggering full securities registration. The same push includes a sandbox-style innovation exemption for round-the-clock, on-chain trading of tokenized equities. None of this waited for Congress. The broader market structure bill is still stalled in the Senate, and the agency is moving on its own.

For agencies building client positioning around a token launch, that is the difference between citing a legal opinion memo and citing an actual rule. A defined capital-raising pathway gives campaign copy something concrete to point to, instead of a patchwork of no-action letters and enforcement history.

The practical move is to read the proposed rule text before Friday's vote, not after. The qualifying conditions in "Regulation Crypto" will decide which client launches fit inside this path and which still need the slower, counsel-heavy route.

If your team has already built a launch around a framework like this one, I want to hear how it changed the timeline.

#Web3Marketing #CryptoRegulation #SEC #DigitalAssets #TokenLaunch

posts.title: Generative speed does not shorten the chain of title.
posts.author: AJAY RAJENDRAN
posts.snippet:
Generative speed does not shorten the chain of title.

It makes rights clearance more urgent.

On 25 August, the company that controls Carl Sagan’s intellectual-property rights sued AI video startup Luma AI in California federal court. The complaint alleges that an audio clip from the documentary series “Cosmos” was used without permission in an advertisement for Luma’s video-generation platform. The allegation has not been adjudicated.

The leadership lesson is not limited to one lawsuit.

AI marketing teams can now create, remix and publish assets faster than traditional approval processes were designed to handle. That speed increases the chance that a recognisable voice, archive clip, image, likeness, soundtrack or brand reference reaches the public before anyone confirms the rights.

“Generated with AI” is not a legal clearance category.

Before creative scale, organisations need a traceable answer to four questions:

Where did every source element come from?

Who owns or controls it?

What licence covers this specific commercial use?

Who approved publication?

The control cannot live only with legal. Marketing operations, agencies, procurement and AI-tool administrators need a shared rights workflow, with source records attached to the final asset and clear escalation for uncertain material.

The reputational risk is especially high when the disputed material belongs to a recognised person, estate or cultural work. The audience will see the association before it sees the legal disclaimer.

AI can compress production time. It cannot compress ownership.

Is rights clearance built into your AI creative workflow—or added after the campaign is ready to launch?

#GenerativeAI #IntellectualProperty #MarketingGovernance #BrandRisk #AICompliance
posts.reason: AI and IP clearance workflow governance is directly relevant to deep-tech and fintech founders we advise on IP assignment and AI Act readiness.

comments.text: The chain-of-title point applies just as much to AI Act compliance as to IP clearance — generating an asset fast doesn't generate a licence, and "trained on public data" is not a rights clearance category either.
In your experience, where does the workflow actually break down most — sourcing the input clip, or the final approval step where someone signs off without seeing the underlying licence?
We do IP assignment and licensing work for tech clients and the recurring problem isn't malice, it's speed: nobody built an escalation path for "uncertain material," so it defaults to publish.

posts.title: Boehringer Ingelheim is seeking to stop Russian pharmaceutical company Groteks/Solopharm from selling Emforix, a generic containing empagliflozin, the active ingredient in Boehring
posts.author: Ольга Мацелюх
posts.snippet:
Boehringer Ingelheim is seeking to stop Russian pharmaceutical company Groteks/Solopharm from selling Emforix, a generic containing empagliflozin, the active ingredient in Boehringer’s Jardiance.

According to Russian industry and legal sources, the relevant patent protection remains valid until November 28, 2029. Boehringer argues that the Russian product entered the market without the patent holder’s consent and has pursued the matter through both the courts and Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service.

The case becomes particularly significant because Groteks is simultaneously seeking a compulsory licence that could allow it to use the patented invention without the patent holder’s voluntary permission.

No final decision granting such a licence had been reported in the cited proceedings, so this should not be presented as an established expropriation of Boehringer’s patent.
But the dispute highlights a broader question for international companies operating in Russia: how predictable is the protection of intellectual property when a local competitor can commercialise a competing product and simultaneously seek legal authority to continue doing so?

For foreign businesses, Russia-related risk is no longer limited to sanctions, reputation or capital controls. The predictability and enforceability of property and intellectual-property rights must also be part of the calculation.

#BoehringerIngelheim #Russia #Pharma #IntellectualProperty #PatentRights #BusinessRisk #ForeignInvestment #InternationalBusiness #DontFundRussianWar #Ukraine
posts.reason: Patent enforceability and compulsory licensing in Russia affects deep-tech exporters, but the post is geopolitically narrow and doesn't invite discussion from our target buyers.

comments.text: Worth flagging that compulsory licensing under Russian Civil Code provisions has been used increasingly since 2022 as a workaround for foreign patent holders unwilling to license voluntarily — it's a distinct legal mechanism from expropriation, but the practical effect on enforceability is similar.

We advise tech clients on IP protection across the EU and the honest answer to your closing question is that predictability was already deteriorating for foreign IP holders in Russia before 2022 — this dispute is just a very visible pharma-sector data point.

posts.title: 12. ROADMAP
posts.author: William Kitchens
posts.snippet:
12. ROADMAP

Phase 1: Build a narrow proof of concept around one biometric or biological use case.

Phase 2: Build and test the consent experience.

Phase 3: Pilot with research, healthcare, or technology organizations.

Phase 4: Expand into permission marketplaces and cooperative governance.

Phase 5: Establish interoperable standards for personal data permissions.

13. LIMITATIONS AND OPEN QUESTIONS: Ownership of personal data is governed differently across jurisdictions and contexts. 

Legal rights, intellectual-property interests, contractual rights, privacy rights, and custodial obligations are not identical.

Accordingly, the platform should not make a universal legal claim that every individual owns every datum in a simple property-law sense.

Instead, the initial product should focus on practical control, transparent permission, enforceable contractual terms where appropriate, and strong privacy protections while legal and policy frameworks continue to evolve.

14. CONCLUSION: The future data economy does not have to choose between innovation and individual agency.

A person should be able to understand what is being requested before saying yes.

They should be able to say no.

They should be able to define the purpose.

They should be able to define the duration.

And where appropriate, they should be able to participate in the economic value created from authorized use.

The fundamental question is simple: Who gets to say yes?

The answer should increasingly be:
The person!

posts.title: The European Commission is putting further pressure on Member States to bring their national anti-money laundering rules fully into line with EU law.
posts.author: Eltoma Legal and Corporate Services
posts.snippet:
The European Commission is putting further pressure on Member States to bring their national anti-money laundering rules fully into line with EU law.
Germany, France and Austria are facing infringement proceedings over the way they have implemented Directive (EU) 2018/1673 on combating money laundering by criminal law.
The Commission’s concerns include national definitions and the rules governing the liability of legal persons — an important issue where money laundering involves companies or other corporate structures.
The three countries have received formal notices and were given two months to respond. If the Commission is not satisfied with the measures taken, it may move to the next stage of the infringement procedure and issue a reasoned opinion.
Spain and Poland are already one step further in the process.
The Commission has issued reasoned opinions to both countries over shortcomings connected with Regulation (EU) 2023/1113, the EU Transfer of Funds Regulation.
The issue is not simply the application of the Regulation itself. Spain and Poland have failed to complete the required changes to the Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive introduced by the Regulation and to notify the necessary national rules on administrative sanctions and other measures.
The Regulation is particularly important for the crypto sector. It extends traceability requirements to transfers of crypto-assets, requiring prescribed information on the originator and beneficiary to accompany relevant transfers — the principle commonly known as the “travel rule”.
Spain and Poland were also given two months to take the necessary action. If the shortcomings remain unresolved, the Commission may refer the cases to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
These proceedings are another sign that the EU’s AML framework is moving from legislative reform to enforcement.
That shift is becoming increasingly relevant for financial institutions, crypto-asset service providers and other regulated businesses. AMLA has already begun operations in Frankfurt, while preparations continue for its future supervisory role under the EU’s new AML architecture.
For businesses operating across several EU jurisdictions, differences in national implementation remain important — but the direction of travel is clear: greater harmonisation, stronger supervision and considerably less tolerance for gaps in AML compliance.
#EU #AML #Compliance #MoneyLaundering #TravelRule #CryptoAssets #FinancialCrime #Regulation #AMLA #ELTOMA
posts.reason: EU AML enforcement against member states and crypto travel rule compliance is directly relevant to CASP authorisation and compliance leads facing MiCA deadlines.

comments.text: The Transfer of Funds Regulation angle is the one CASPs should watch most closely — the travel rule obligations under 2023/1113 apply regardless of where national AMLD transposition stands, so gaps in Spain or Poland's domestic sanctions regime don't excuse a CASP's own originator/beneficiary data duties.

Do you know whether the Commission's reasoned opinions to Spain and Poland specifically flag the administrative sanctions regime for crypto-asset service providers, or is that still bundled into the broader AMLD4 shortfall?

We're seeing this play out for CASPs directly — travel rule compliance obligations are already live even where the host state's own transposition and sanctioning framework is still catching up, which leaves an awkward enforcement gap for firms trying to do the right thing.

For most people, the latest announcement from BitMart is industry news.

For us, it is part of the ATEG story.

When we decided to list ATEG.DV on BitMart, we did not choose an unknown platform. We chose an exchange that had operated for years, built an international name and at one point ranked around number 16 on CoinMarketCap.

From the outside, it represented reach, experience and continuity.

We went through the entire process. We completed the preparations, coordinated the technical requirements, worked with our market making team and did everything expected from us as a serious listed project.

Then, after only around six and a half weeks of trading, operations were restricted.

Six and a half weeks.

That was never enough time for ATEG.DV to establish a genuine market, reach the wider BitMart user base or develop the visibility that a listing of this level was supposed to create.

We were affected by what happened.

But we were not broken by it.

A high ranking is not a guarantee.

A recognized name is not a guarantee.

Years of operation are not a guarantee.

The only foundation you can truly control is what you build yourself.

I welcome this step.

But affected users and listed projects now need more than another announcement. They need transparency, accountability and a concrete path forward.

comments.text: The liquid staking classification gap is real: MiCAR simply wasn't drafted with restaking and derivative claims on staked assets in mind, so issuers are stuck mapping a novel instrument onto categories built for utility, e-money and asset-referenced tokens. A sector taxonomy is genuinely useful groundwork for ESMA and NCAs, since right now every CASP is making its own call.

Does the taxonomy attempt to draw a line between liquid staking tokens that are pure derivative claims versus those that carry governance or yield features closer to an ART? That distinction is where we've seen CASP authorisation conversations stall.

We've had the same conversation with clients trying to list staking-derivative tokens under MiCA - the white paper duties are clear enough, but which regime applies before you even get to notification is genuinely unsettled. Good to see it move from roundtable to published research.

posts.title: 🎯 Institutional compliance frameworks operating across Europe frequently confuse technical alignment with judicial enforceability. The publication titled The Blueprint to Complianc
posts.author: Gábor Almási
posts.snippet:
🎯 Institutional compliance frameworks operating across Europe frequently confuse technical alignment with judicial enforceability. The publication titled The Blueprint to Compliance Defining the Final Level of the Legal Framework Edition 10 illustrates how administrative expectations deviate from statutory certainty. While the legal architecture spans three distinct levels, the proliferation of soft law at Level 3 creates an illusion of supervisory harmony without offering legal protection during criminal litigation.

Under the prospective authority of AMLA, Level 3 guidelines set uniform standards across jurisdictions, yet these non binding instruments cannot amend primary Level 1 statutes. Obliged entities face a rigid comply or explain mechanism that presents exactly two options, requiring institutions either to demonstrate complete alignment or to articulate written justifications for deviation. This binary requirement transforms voluntary technical standards into quasi mandatory enforcement benchmarks during regulatory audits.

From an evidentiary perspective, supervisory bodies increasingly rely on informal administrative guidance to establish negligence, whereas defense counsel can easily challenge non binding measures before national courts. When complex financial structures operate through multiple jurisdictions, judicial outcomes depend strictly on statutory definitions rather than technical administrative recommendations. This structural friction exposes financial institutions to significant legal liability when their internal controls satisfy administrative guidelines but fail statutory thresholds of proof.

Regulatory effectiveness ultimately depends on statutory clarity rather than administrative volume.

#AML #Compliance #FinancialCrime #AMLA #RegTech #FIAU
posts.reason: Serious discussion of AML/AMLA compliance and regulatory framework complexity speaks directly to compliance officers and financial institutions navigating regulatory enforcement.

comments.text: This is the right way to frame it: AMLA's Level 3 guidance sets supervisory expectation, not statutory obligation, and a comply-or-explain mechanism doesn't change that a court still tests conduct against the Level 1 text. We see the same tension in MiCA - ESMA guidelines shape how NCAs review a white paper, but they can't substitute for the statutory disclosure duties themselves.

In practice, have you seen defence counsel successfully get a finding of negligence overturned by pointing to the non-binding status of Level 3 guidance, or does the comply-or-explain record end up doing the persuasive work regardless of its formal status?

We run into an analogous problem advising CASP applicants - ESMA's technical standards and guidelines shape what an NCA expects on the file, but when a client asks whether following them is a legal safe harbour, the honest answer is no, and that gap matters more than most compliance functions want to admit.

Before you sign: what founders must understand!

Jēkabs S. Venture Faculty Founders Unchained

https://lnkd.in/d9aR4but

Raising capital isn't just about the pitch — it's about understanding the rules you're agreeing to before you even realize you're agreeing to them.

In this video, I break down the layers of rules every founder needs to understand when going through an investment process. First, the process rules — how you approach investors, how you communicate during due diligence, and how you follow up, all shaped by basic business ethics. Second, the legal layer — what the law dictates around company governance, operations, and compliance, rules that are largely fixed and hard to change. Third, the contractual layer — the terms you actively negotiate with investors, defining your rights, obligations, and the nature of the relationship you're entering into for the life of the investment.

Understanding these three layers — process, law, and contract — is essential for any founder navigating a fundraising round. This isn't just legal housekeeping; it's the foundation of how you'll operate with your investors for years to come.

If you're a founder preparing to raise, or already deep in a round, this breakdown will help you see the fundraising process with much more clarity.

🔷 PHASE 2

POST 6.
GOVERNANCE & COMPLIANCE PROTECTION

Building Controls Before Complexity

Series 2.
PROTECTION.
The Reality Behind Survival & Sustainability

The Missing Layer Between Growth and Longevity
---
At the early stage, 
a few people may handle almost everything.

Founder decides.
Team executes.
Everyone knows everyone.

But growth changes the equation.
- More money.
- More employees.
- More customers.
- More vendors.
- More investors.
- More markets.

And with complexity comes the need for clear rules and accountability.

Governance protection means creating systems that answer.
→ Who can make which decision?
→ Who approves spending?
→ Who owns the risk?
→ Who has access to sensitive information?
→ How are conflicts handled?
→ What must be documented?
→ What happens when something goes wrong?

Compliance is part of the same protection layer.

It helps ensure the startup respects the laws, regulations, contracts and obligations that apply to its business.

The mistake is waiting until the organization becomes large.

By then, informal practices may already be deeply embedded.

A better approach is.
Start simple 
→ define responsibilities 
→ document key processes 
→ create controls 
→ review them as the business grows.

Governance should not become bureaucracy.

Good governance should make responsibility clearer, decisions safer and growth more sustainable.

Because the bigger the startup becomes, the more expensive weak controls can become.
---
Governance does not stop entrepreneurship.
It protects entrepreneurship from becoming organizational chaos.

What should a growing startup formalize first — decision-making, finance, access, compliance or accountability?

Controls are easier to build before complexity arrives.

Next Part

— Bringing Funding, Valuation, Product, Technology, Founder & Governance Protection Together.

posts.title: Not every auditor appointment is simply a reg flag. Sometime it could be regulatory compliance.
posts.author: Chandan Dangi
posts.snippet:
Not every auditor appointment is simply a reg flag. Sometime it could be regulatory compliance.


At first when I went through this section while reading VBL's annual report, I came across the name Sanjay Grover & Associates.


First thing came in my mind,

Did VBL change its auditor?

So, I checked the actual filings, and found something valuable and interesting.


There are two types of auditors involved here,


1. Statutory Auditors

J.C Bhalla & Co.
O.P. Bagla & Co. LLP

In Statutory auditors, their primary role is to audit VBL's financial statements.
→ Revenue 
→ Expenses
→ Assets & Liabilities 
→ Cash flows
→ Accounting policies 

These are the auditors most investors usually think about when they hear the word “auditor".


2. Secretarial Auditor:

That is exactly where Sanjay Grover & Associates comes in.  Secretarial auditor's role is different.

Sanjay Grover & Associates examine whether the company is complying with;

 →Companies Act requirements
 →SEBI regulations
 → Corporate governance requirements
 → Board & committee procedures
 → Statutory filings and records
 → Other applicable corporate laws


So, Sanjay Grover & Associates didn't replace J.C. Bhalla or O.P. Bagla, they both have different role in VBL.


But then why did VBL appoint them for another 5 years?

After reading VBL's AGM notice, appointment was made in the context of the amended regulation 24A of SEBI LODR, which require listed companies to appoint/ reappoint a peer-reviewed secretarial auditor for the perscribed term.

One more intereting thing I found.

Sanjay Grover & Associates weren't new to VBL.

Sanjay Grover & Associates were already working with VBL a its Secreterial Auditor.

So, this wasn't because the previous auditor resigned or there was any disagreement.

VBL was simply formally appointing the same firm again under the new regulatory requirements.


Is it a red flag?
 
Absolute answer is no. I also found the same with another large listed company, Britannia has the similar pattern, its existing secretarial auditor was also continued under the new five year framework.


My takeaway:

I believe we should not create a governance red flag before checking what actually happened.

New auditor name in the corporate filling doen't automatically means something went wrong. We should identify first what type of auditor it is, what changed and why.

So, VBL's auditor history doen't currently raise a major concern.

posts.title: The 11th-Hour Licence Scramble
posts.author: Sarah Borg Bonnici
posts.snippet:
The 11th-Hour Licence Scramble

In the final stretch of a new specialist pharmacy or CL3 lab build, a common scene unfolds: builders are packing up, the facility is practically done – and someone asks, “Have we sorted the licence and validation?” Cue the collective face-palm.

The truth is, getting a facility licensed and fully validated is as big a job as building it – but it’s often treated as an afterthought.

Pain points we’ve witnessed when compliance and validation work is under-resourced or started too late include:
• Last-minute documentation panic: Realising close to handover that hundreds of pages of SOPs, validation protocols, and maintenance plans haven’t been written or approved. Suddenly everyone is scrambling to produce “paperwork” that should have been developed in parallel with design and construction.
• Delayed openings: The facility might be physically complete, but regulators (like the MHRA or HSE) need to see evidence – from commissioning results to training records – before granting approval. If those weren’t methodically prepared, the lab can sit idle for weeks or months awaiting certification, costing the hospital money and lost service capacity.
• Operational staff overload: Often the same key people who delivered the project are asked to handle validation and licensing at the end – on top of their day jobs. Without dedicated focus, things slip. We’ve seen quality managers brought in too late, trying to retrofit compliance to a design that is already built, which is a recipe for frustration.

Our take? “Begin with the end in mind” isn’t just a slogan – it means treating Day‑1 operation and licensing as equal to construction from the start. On our projects, we push for an integrated validation plan early: mapping out who’s responsible for each compliance item, and resourcing it properly (e.g. bringing in a validation lead or quality assurance specialist from day one).

We also align the design with the end regulatory requirements so we’re not undoing work later. The goal is that when the build is done, the binders are done too – and the inspectors’ questions have already been answered. A calm, thorough commissioning and validation phase ensures that when you cut the ribbon, you can actually open the doors to patients and staff – not just to more auditors.

posts.title: De nieuwste PISA-resultaten laten opnieuw zien hoe cruciaal een sterke taalbasis is voor de onderwijskansen van leerlingen. Nederlandse leerlingen lijken in leesvaardigheid opnieuw
posts.author: Jeroen Aarssen
posts.snippet:
De nieuwste PISA-resultaten laten opnieuw zien hoe cruciaal een sterke taalbasis is voor de onderwijskansen van leerlingen. Nederlandse leerlingen lijken in leesvaardigheid opnieuw verder achterop te raken bij leeftijdgenoten in andere landen. Een land als Ierland laat zien hoe het wél kan.

Het geheim? Waarschijnlijk niet één briljante leesmethode. Niet nóg een tijdelijk taalproject. En ook niet simpelweg meer uren taal. De interessante les uit Ierland is het investeren in een langdurige, samenhangende visie: langjarig werken aan taal en rekenen. Inzetten op het vakmanschap van leraren. Extra ondersteuning waar de achterstanden het grootst zijn. Curriculum, didactiek en professionalisering met elkaar verbinden. En consequent blijven volgen, leren en verbeteren. Vooral de relatief hoge ondergrens is interessant: Ierland slaagt erin te voorkomen dat grote groepen leerlingen onvoldoende leesvaardig worden.

Dat raakt precies aan wat wij bij CPS Onderwijsontwikkeling en advies bedoelen met Taalkrachtig Onderwijs. Taal is namelijk niet alleen iets van de taalles. Taal is ook niet alleen lezen. Meer aandacht voor productieve vaardigheden als spreken en schrijven is cruciaal. Taal is de infrastructuur van leren. Een leerling heeft taal nodig om een tekst te begrijpen, maar óók om een rekenstrategie uit te leggen, een historisch vraagstuk te onderzoeken, kennis op te bouwen, argumenten te formuleren en gedachten onder woorden te brengen.
Daarom werken we niet alleen aan de taalvaardige leerling. We werken aan de combinatie van de taalvaardige leerling, de taalbewuste leerkracht en de taalrijke school.

En misschien moeten we daarin nog ambitieuzer zijn. Niet vragen: welke taalinterventie heeft deze school nodig? Maar wel: welke infrastructuur heeft deze school nodig om over drie jaar aantoonbaar sterker taalonderwijs te geven — en dat daarna zelfstandig te blijven verbeteren?

Dat betekent: eerst goed analyseren. Samen prioriteiten kiezen. Leerkrachten toerusten. Taal verbinden met alle vakken. Een leerteam en schoolleiding in positie brengen. Kijken wat er daadwerkelijk in de klas verandert. En vervolgens borgen. Dat is ook de planmatige aanpak die we binnen Taalkrachtig Onderwijs hanteren.

De ambitie?
Minder leerlingen die door de taalbodem zakken. Meer leerlingen die taal krachtig kunnen gebruiken om te denken, leren en deelnemen. Van interventie naar infrastructuur. Van taalles naar taal in iedere les. Van tijdelijke ondersteuning naar duurzaam professioneel vermogen.
Dat is voor mij misschien wel de belangrijkste Ierse les voor het Nederlandse onderwijs.

posts.title: Every law firm I speak to believes their workflows are unique.
posts.author: Dom Conte
posts.snippet:
Every law firm I speak to believes their workflows are unique.

Almost none of them are.

I've sat through probably fifty discovery sessions where a firm explains their bespoke process for matter intake, or document review, or client onboarding. And every time, about twenty minutes in, I realise I've heard this exact workflow described by another firm, sometimes using the same internal terminology.

The belief in uniqueness isn't vanity. It comes from somewhere real. Lawyers are trained to find distinctions, to spot the clause that's different, the precedent that doesn't quite fit. That's what makes them excellent lawyers. But it also means when they look at their own operations, they see complexity and specificity everywhere, even when the underlying process is basically the same as the firm down the road.

This matters because it drives a particular kind of building. Firms commission bespoke platforms shaped around every internal quirk, and end up with tools so tailored to "how we work" that they're fragile, expensive to maintain, and frankly a bit miserable to use. The firms getting genuine adoption right now are doing something counterintuitive. They're building for people, not for lawyers. Generic-feeling interfaces, standard patterns, minimal customisation.

I reckon the firms that stop treating their lawyers as a special category of user will be the ones whose tech actually gets used.

posts.title: SUPREME COURT CLARIFIES A CRITICAL TAX APPEAL ISSUE
posts.author: Muhammad Salman
posts.snippet:
SUPREME COURT CLARIFIES A CRITICAL TAX APPEAL ISSUE

Can Commissioner (Appeals) simply send a tax case back for a “fresh assessment”?
The Supreme Court of Pakistan says: No not under the post-2005 version of section 129(1)(a).
In Commissioner Inland Revenue (Legal Zone), LTO Lahore v. M/s Seven Star Sugar Mills (Pvt.) Ltd., reported as 2026 SCMR 69, the Supreme Court examined the powers of the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 129(1)(a) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

What was the dispute?
The assessment had been amended under section 122(5A).
The Commissioner (Appeals) found the assessment order invalid and annulled it—but then remanded the matter for fresh proceedings.
The taxpayer challenged this approach.
The Supreme Court examined the history of section 129 and found that the Finance Act, 2005 removed the express power of the Commissioner (Appeals) to set aside an assessment and direct a fresh assessment.

⚖️ What can CIR(A) do?
Under the applicable section 129(1)(a), the Commissioner (Appeals) may:
✅ Confirm the assessment
✅ Modify the assessment
✅ Annul the assessment
✅ Conduct or cause further enquiries where required
But the Court held that CIR(A) cannot go beyond the statutory powers and remand the matter to the lower forum for a fresh assessment.

💡 Why does this matter?
This is extremely important when reviewing an appellate order.
A taxpayer should not automatically accept a CIR(A) order saying:

“Assessment annulled — case remanded for fresh assessment.”
The jurisdiction and statutory authority for that direction must be examined.
The Supreme Court also reaffirmed an important principle of fiscal law:
Taxing statutes must be interpreted according to the words enacted by the legislature. Courts cannot add words or powers that the statute does not contain.

Practical takeaway for Tax Practitioners
When reviewing a tax appeal order, don't focus only on “tax demand reduced or cancelled.”
Check:
What exactly has CIR(A) ordered?
If the order involves a remand, fresh assessment, further proceedings or restoration of the case, examine whether the Commissioner (Appeals) actually possessed jurisdiction under the applicable version of section 129.
A technically incorrect appellate order can create another round of unnecessary tax proceedings.
📚 Case: Commissioner Inland Revenue (Legal Zone), LTO Lahore v. M/s Seven Star Sugar Mills (Pvt.) Ltd.
Citation: 2026 SCMR 69 | 2026 PTD 90
Key provisions: Sections 122(5A), 129(1)(a) & 133(1), Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

Debt above $40 trillion, with interest costs climbing faster than revenues.
De‑dollarisation at the margins, as central banks diversify reserves and BRICS builds alternative payment rails.

Fiscal and institutional discipline – credible plans to rein in deficits and protect the rule of law.
Restraint in using financial and military power – fewer blanket sanctions, fewer regime‑change impulses, more respect for other nations’ autonomy.
Partnership over bullying – working with large, independent democracies that can help steady the system.

Opposed a common BRICS currency.

posts.title: On 3 September 2026 the European Commission adopted its Guidelines on exclusionary abuses of dominance under Article 102 TFEU. C(2026) 6118 final. 77 pages.
posts.author: Mykola Shyyan
posts.snippet:
On 3 September 2026 the European Commission adopted its Guidelines on exclusionary abuses of dominance under Article 102 TFEU. C(2026) 6118 final. 77 pages.

Most commentary framed it as a Big Tech story. Read the text and a different picture emerges: the case law behind the access provisions comes from fuel and energy infrastructure, not platforms.

Three points for anyone working with grids and pipelines.

1. The Bronner shield is gone for regulated operators. For thirty years infrastructure owners met access requests with the Bronner test: prove the asset is indispensable, prove refusal eliminates all effective competition. Footnote 376 narrows it sharply. Where an undertaking's autonomy over access is limited by obligations imposed by legislation, regulation or contract, it cannot be regarded as "owning" the input at all. The strict test does not apply; the general framework does. The authority cited: Lukoil Bulgaria (C-245/24, 18 December 2025) — a case on access to fuel storage infrastructure.

A TSO or DSO under a statutory duty to grant access no longer has that shield.

2. Delay is now a named example of abuse. Paragraph 182(d)(ii) lists as a possible access restriction the failure to respond to access requests in a timely manner, or delaying negotiations and the signing of access contracts. Paragraph 181 adds: access restrictions can distort competition even where the input is not indispensable.

For any market where connection requests sit unanswered for months, that is a very specific sentence.

3. Compliance with sector regulation is not a defence. Paragraph 12: conduct found to comply with other EU or national legislation may still infringe Article 102. Grid codes and competition law are parallel regimes, not alternatives.

Why this reaches Ukraine. Not through direct effect — the Guidelines are EU soft law. Through the Energy Community Treaty. Article 18(1)(b) prohibits abuse of a dominant position in network-transported energy. Article 18(2) requires such conduct to be assessed "on the basis of criteria arising from the application of the rules of Articles 81, 82 and 87" of the EC Treaty — Article 82 being today's Article 102 TFEU. The Association Agreement points the same way: Article 253(2)(a) defines EU competition law as Articles 101, 102 and 106 TFEU; Article 256 commits Ukraine to approximating enforcement practice, not just legislation.

That is not a binding rule for the AMCU or a Ukrainian court. It is a recognised interpretive standard Ukraine has already accepted twice over.

Two details most reviews miss: the Guidelines contain no reference to the Digital Markets Act, none at all; and the 2009 Guidance is withdrawn only 30 days after publication in the Official Journal — which has not happened yet.

Full analysis, with the Ukrainian angle, in the first comment.

Canada’s defence industry is diversifying fast — and moving beyond traditional U.S. partners brings new regulatory, security and commercial realities that every supplier must factor into bids and contracts.
Canadian defence companies are focusing on quantum, AI/autonomy, uncrewed systems, advanced ISR, munitions, shipbuilding, cyber, and space—all driven by procurement priorities for sovereign supply, interoperability with allies, stronger cyber and controlled‑goods requirements, and industrial‑benefit commitments. 
Growth markets include NATO/Europe, the Indo‑Pacific, Five Eyes partners, and large domestic programs (icebreakers, shipbuilding, munitions), while dual‑use commercial markets (space, critical infrastructure, emergency response) provide scale and export pathways.
Key considerations for companies entering non‑ITAR markets 
• Canadian export controls still apply — export permits under the EIPA are required for military goods, tech and services. 
• U.S. law can still reach your product — U.S.‑origin parts, software or data may trigger ITAR/EAR re‑export rules. 
• Do a provenance audit up front — map every component, library and licence to its country of origin. 
• Tighten end‑user and sanctions screening — screen customers, agents and intermediaries against Canadian, U.S., UN and other lists. 
• Update contracts and flow‑downs — include export‑control clauses, re‑export prohibitions and audit rights. 
• Plan for local industrial requirements — offsets, local content and sustainment commitments must be reconciled with export controls. 
• Raise your cyber and supply‑chain posture — CGP registration, CPCSC/cyber controls and secure data hosting are increasingly mandatory. 
• Define servicing and spares rules — in‑country repairs and parts shipments often require separate licences and controls.
Diversifying markets is a major growth opportunity — but compliance, provenance and security planning must happen before you bid.

NDA with a Legal Services Provider: Why Broadening "Confidential Information" Matters

1. Expanding the Definition of Confidential Information
✓ Legal firms handle information "in process", without formal protection protocols in advance

✓ Legal firms hold information of multiple clients, including potential competitors

Quien no aprende a leer comprendiendo, a razonar matemáticamente o a interpretar científicamente el mundo queda mucho más expuesto a la pobreza, la dependencia, la manipulación y la exclusión.

El fracaso de país que certifica el informe #PISA afecta profunda y radicalmente a la igualdad de oportunidades. Es, por tanto y además, una vulneración de sus derechos fundamentales y del principio de bien superior del menor.

Hemos construido un sistema de educación sentimental, en el que el cuidado emocional ha ido ocupando el espacio que corresponde a enseñar. Formamos ciudadanos con dificultades para comprender y argumentar, y profesionales cuya preparación no se corresponde con la complejidad del mundo en el que ya viven.

La banalización del currículo, la rendición a lo emocional, no es sino otra traición al país y a nuestro futuro común.

La IA, las pantallas y la crisis de atención golpean todos los sistemas educativos del mundo, por no hablar de la extraordinaria disminución de la natalidad y el cambio de paradigma de la docencia clásica. Pero es netamente español el sectarismo político y el ineficiente fraccionamiento administrativo.

En las próximas elecciones autonómicas, cada programa electoral debe explicar en detalle cómo garantizará que todos los alumnos de la educación obligatoria sean competitivos a nivel europeo en las competencias básicas del siglo XXI, con independencia del código postal.

Esa reconversión exige concitar voluntades y conocimiento, y ser diseñada sin dogmas y desde la evidencia. La condición, como en toda reconversión, es que no haya perdedores. Ni profesores ni alumnos, ni padres ni administraciones, ni la escuela pública ni la concertada ni la privada, ni un territorio u otro.

posts.title: The estate planning gap in cryptoassets is not valuation. It is access.
posts.author: MyAssurety
posts.snippet:
The estate planning gap in cryptoassets is not valuation. It is access.

HMRC's position is settled and unremarkable: cryptoassets form part of the estate "in much the same way as other assets, such as bank accounts, property, shares, and investments", with a date of death value reported on the return.

The practical problem sits one step further on. Where the assets are believed inaccessible, HMRC asks for an explanation as to why, and what the value is believed to be, within the additional information box of the IHT400. Cryptoassets do not qualify for loss on sale relief either. So an estate can carry a reporting obligation for an asset no personal representative can reach, with no relief for the shortfall.

The drafting point that follows is the one most often missed. The access instruction cannot sit in the will, because a will becomes a public document once probate is granted and a copy can be ordered by anyone for £16. The appropriate home is a letter of wishes or an equivalent private memorandum stored alongside it, with the key itself held separately again.

For advisers: the review question on any estate holding digital assets is whether the personal representatives would know the asset exists at all, and whether the pointer to it has been drafted into a public document by accident.

Sources: HMRC Cryptoassets Manual CRYPTO25000, GOV.UK, read 8 September 2026.

posts.title: At the end of last year, a rumor spread fast through the Chinese Web3 community: police in cities like Hangzhou and Chengdu were allegedly stopping people on the street or knocking
posts.author: Honglin Liu
posts.snippet:
At the end of last year, a rumor spread fast through the Chinese Web3 community: police in cities like Hangzhou and Chengdu were allegedly stopping people on the street or knocking on doors, and if a crypto app or wallet assets were found on the phone, demanding an "immediate transfer." Many practitioners were genuinely shaken. After cross-checking with multiple sources, our criminal defense team concluded this is very likely a rumor blown out of proportion — a self-media tactic, not a real policy.

Instead of feeding the fear, we broke it down with legal reasoning. Why doesn't "confiscate on sight" hold up in law? Two basics: street interrogation power is not arbitrary search power — unlocking a phone to inspect private apps without a search warrant is procedurally unlawful; and disposing of seized assets follows an extremely strict process — forcing a transfer without a case filing or seizure order could expose the officers themselves to charges like abuse of power or even extortion. Regulation is tightening, yes, but such overreach can never be the norm. If the extreme case ever happens: verify identity, no transfer without paperwork, only to official accounts, appeal afterwards. Fear comes from the unknown; safety comes from professionalism.
